title: The seventh rooms
hook: at the center Martha and Mary work together

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sitivit: the ache of being close and not yet, a sign that God is near. Today, at last, the center of the castle.

After a week of walking through rooms, you'd expect the center to be a throne room, or a cloud, or somewhere you never have to come back from. You'd expect the saint who reaches it to float off and stop doing laundry. Teresa of Ávila reached these rooms herself, she believed, and her life didn't float anywhere. She kept founding convents, riding in bumpy wagons, arguing with officials, writing letters about money and leaky roofs. She says that's exactly the point.
screen: `YOU'D EXPECT A THRONE ROOM.` → `TERESA KEPT RIDING IN WAGONS.` → `THAT'S THE POINT.`

segments.voice: First, the marriage. Teresa uses the language of love and marriage for the deepest union with God, following the Song of Songs and a long line of saints. In the sixth rooms the soul was betrothed. Here it's married, and the union doesn't come and go anymore. She gives two pictures. Two candles can be held together into one flame, then pulled apart. But rain falling into a river becomes the river. You can't find the raindrop again. Second, the peace. Trouble doesn't stop: there are still trials and noise around the edges of the castle. But in the center there's a stillness nothing reaches. Third, Martha and Mary. In Luke's Gospel, Martha rushes around serving while her sister Mary sits at Jesus's feet and listens. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful, and art troubled about many things: But one thing is necessary." People have used that story for centuries to rank prayer over work. Teresa won't. At the very center, she says, Martha and Mary must work together, so that the Lord is welcomed and fed. Fourth, the purpose. This is why all this prayer exists, Teresa says: to give birth to good works. Not feelings. Works. Look back at this week: a crystal castle with prayer as the door, the struggling second rooms, the careful third, two fountains, a silkworm, the long ache of the sixth. And at the center, not an escape from life, but a marriage that sends you back into it.
screen: `A RAINDROP FALLS INTO A RIVER.` · `STILLNESS AT THE CENTER.` · `MARTHA AND MARY, TOGETHER.` · `PRAYER GIVES BIRTH TO WORKS.` · then, large: `BUT ONE THING IS NECESSARY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next task waiting for you: an email, a meal, a shift, a chore. Sit with it a moment the way Mary sat, quiet, before you rise to do it the way Martha would. If you pray, offer the task to God before you begin; if you don't, choose who the work is for.
Spiritual marriage. Teresa's name for the union at the center of the castle, like rain falling into a river, which sends the soul back out to serve. Today's word.
Your line: martha and mary together. One listens, one serves, and both welcome the Lord. Day two hundred fifty-two, done.

howItsDone: Catholic teachers point to Teresa's seventh dwelling places to show that the goal of contemplative prayer is not escape but love in action, and Carmelite communities join long hours of prayer with daily work and service.
